extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and general listeners interested in personal storytelling comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting and performing personal, autobiographical stand-up or one-man-show material that turns painful or embarrassing life events into comedy and narrative performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy is 'tragedy plus time'
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is tragedy plus time — painful events often become funny only after some time has passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no set time; the interval varies by person and circumstance. Be mindful that people close to you may still be uncomfortable even when you find it funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make private/embarrassing things public (secret public journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take personal, embarrassing, or private experiences and put them 'out there' as material (the author's 'Secret Public Journal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This vulnerability can be the core of your comedy, but consider consequences for family/friends (they may be tempted not to read or feel exposed). Ask permission when necessary and be prepared for mixed reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk about things that make people uncomfortable
rubrics_metrics.description: Good comedy addresses uncomfortable or taboo subjects rather than avoiding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using uncomfortable material helps audiences 'come to grips' with subjects; comics should be prepared for pushback (e.g., audience members declaring something 'not funny'). Strong performers defend their choices when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generic mimicry — cultivate originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't sound like the prevalent or iconic comedians ('mimeographs' of Jerry Seinfeld or Mitch Hedberg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously stop copying influences; develop a distinct voice and point of view. Imitation is a common early-stage anti-pattern to outgrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good monologue is about more than its ostensible subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-person story or monologue should use a central incident as an anchor but expand to other themes (e.g., romance, family relationships, short courses on disorders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the story lead to related emotional or thematic material so the piece feels layered and not narrowly tethered to a single event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, specific detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete details (dates, places, physical descriptions) make stories vivid and believable (example: jump through a closed window at the La Quinta Inn in Walla Walla).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity grounds surreal or extreme actions and helps audiences visualize and empathize; small sensory details can become recurring bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability and honesty to connect with audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Being open about fears, flaws, and anxieties helps build rapport and comedic payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honesty can be painful but resonates; balancing self-exposure with craft is key (e.g., telling about cancer or sleepwalking candidly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pain and humor — timing for turning trauma into jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't rush converting traumatic or painful material into humor; the performer must judge when the subject is ready to be treated comically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity to the emotional weight of material is required; what’s funny to the performer may still hurt close others. Test material carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of musical parody and comedic songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Songs and parodies (Christian rock parody, 'Medium Man', etc.) are useful devices in a comedic set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical bits can diversify pacing and tone; genre-parody works by mimicking trends and subverting expectations. Keep songs tight and relevant to your persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage live performance energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Live versions carry a different energy than studio-recorded pieces and can be especially compelling for storytelling comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the implications of releasing live vs. studio recordings (audience reaction can enhance a piece but may affect later releases). Use live dynamics intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure and arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Build clear narrative arcs—even in stand-up—so stories have setup, escalation, and payoff (examples: birth/death of a romance, portrait of a father).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think like a storyteller: arrange beats to reveal character, stakes, and transformation rather than only punchline-after-punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop and collaborate with trusted editors/producers
rubrics_metrics.description: Refine stories through collaboration (directors, producers, experienced storytellers like Ira Glass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative feedback improves clarity, pacing, and selection of the final form (live vs. studio). Be open to guidance but keep your voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't let audience gatekeepers dictate what is funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers decide comedic value; audience members may object, but comic intent and context matter (illustrated by Joan Rivers' response to hecklers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stand by well-crafted choices while remaining adaptable; know your boundaries for offending vs. alienating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physicality and visual elements in storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical actions and images (e.g., breaking through a window, glass shards, wearing a sleep sack) add comedic and dramatic weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe or enact physical moments to enhance believability and visceral humor; props and physical recall can create memorable images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition and contrast as comedic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair incongruous elements (e.g., eating pizza and watching the news before sleep) to create absurdity and humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts highlight irrational behavior and underline comic premises; use them to sharpen observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring motifs/props can anchor bits
rubrics_metrics.description: Small recurring items (sleep sack, mittens, pizza habit) become running jokes and help cohesion across material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce motifs early and bring them back for payoff; they can also serve as metaphors for character traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about factual/medical details when invoking them
rubrics_metrics.description: When using medical or technical explanations (e.g., REM behavior disorder, dopamine deficiency), avoid 'bastardizing' facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate framing or disclaimers if unsure; respect listeners who may know the details (and avoid misinforming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target your platform/audience strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose venues and media that fit your storytelling style (e.g., This American Life listeners favor narrative comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different audiences value different approaches—tailor material and form accordingly (podcast, live theater, clubs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-comedic delivery and stagecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage business and meta-comments (e.g., 'Please don't clap', deliberate pauses) control audience reaction and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-aware asides and micro-timing to shape laughs and breathing room; small cues manage crowd dynamics.
